newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-FRANCE HIT ROCK BOTTOM AS LONG UNBEATEN RUN ENDS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FRANCE HIT ROCK BOTTOM AS LONG UNBEATEN RUN ENDS.

text.p: For Aime Jacquet's France, preparing to host the 1998 World Cup finals, things can only get better after the low point of ignominious defeat against Denmark which ended their remarkable 30-match unbeaten run.
"For the first time since I've been the coach the French team had me worried. During one half we were non-existent," a disappointed Jacquet said after Saturday's 1-0 defeat in Copenhagen.
"I'd never seen that before. There are situations I can't tolerate. The whole state of mind that we've managed to build over a period of time was shattered."
Jacquet will be looking for a vast improvement when France, only playing friendlies in the World Cup build-up while their rivals compete in qualifiers, visit Portugal for their next match in January.

France's team spirit helped them build an unbeaten run that began with Jacquet's first match, a 1-0 win over Italy in Naples in February 1994 following the country's failure to qualify for the World Cup finals in the United States.
It was only the fifth time in 31 matches that France fell behind. The four previous occasions were at home, the last in February 1995 when France recovered to beat Greece 3-1.

But then the playmaking duo of Zinedine Zidane and Youri Djorkaeff, which went off the boil during Euro 96 in England in June, was in-form and contributed six of the nine goals scored in those four recoveries.
The Denmark defeat was preceeded by failure to reach the Euro 96 final in Jacquet's first major tournamant.

But elimination came about in a penalty shootout after a goalless draw with the Czech Republic, leaving Jacquet with serious questions concerning his attack but none over arguably the soundest defence in the competition.

In Copenhagen on Saturday, one of his defensive stalwarts Marcel Desailly had easily his worst game in French colours -- appropriately their second choice white on this occassion as against the Czechs in Manchester.
That the AC Milan player was without his habitual centre-back partner Laurent Blanc, playing for Barcelona, highlights two of Jacquet's chief problems: Availability and motivation.
Only four of France's starting line-up against the Danes play their club football in the French league.

Some of those who joined Italian clubs in the off-season, notably Zidane at Juventus and Djorkaeff with Internazionale, are only just emerging from a difficult settling in period in a new environment.

Furthermore, it is an environment rich in challenges -- top European club competition as well as arguably the world's most demanding first division -- far outweighing friendlies for France when the carrot of the World Cup is still so distant.

Add to that the fact that FIFA have turned down Jacquet's request for the same benefits for his friendlies of a five-day period with his players ahead of at least five matches in a year officially afforded to coaches ahead of competitive games.
But despite comments to the contrary by himself and the players, Jacquet can draw positive conclusions from the defeat.
He played Djorkaeff alone up front in a role that does not suit a player most comfortable in the "hole" behind the outright striker.
"France will never again play a match like that, I'm sure," Djorkaeff said. "We'll do as we did against Mexico and Turkey. We're sufficiently intelligent to react immediately."

In their last friendly at home to Turkey last month, France overcame another slow start in which they could have fallen behind and a single closely marked striker by attacking from deep positions with Blanc and midfielder Reynald Pedros breaking through to score the first two goals in a 4-0 win.
Jacquet said: "I assure you that if we'd played Brazil I wouldn't have done that (play Djorkaeff up front).

"Now, when you get the chance to have such a sharp and skilled player in front of goal, it's something you have to try out. At a precise moment in the World Cup if he has to save the France team, he may be compelled to play like that.
"When we go for the World Cup, I don't want to have any regrets and, on the contrary, to have tested a lot of different situations."
